(Received 23 December 2013; accepted 9 March 2014; published online 19 March 2014)

In this study, we developed a flexible energy harvester that uses the frequency up-conversion mechanism. The harvester is composed of a flexible piezoelectric cantilever and substrate, and it can scavenge energy from deformation or strain by converting it into a mechanical vibration of the cantilever. We found experimentally that the output voltage of the harvester not affected by an input frequency as long as the strain was large enough, and there was no lower limit of the input frequency. The critical strain, i.e., the threshold radius of curvature of the harvester, could be modulated by adjusting magnetic force; therefore, it is possible to optimally apply the harvester to various deformation ranges. The maximum and average power density at $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ of input frequency was measured to be $\bar { 3 } 2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { W / c m } ^ { 2 }$ and $6 . 8 \ \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for a resistive load of $1 0 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ . $©$ 2014 AIP Publishing LLC. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4869130]

With the increasingly widespread use of wireless electronic devices, piezoelectric energy harvesting from ambient vibration or human motion has attracted considerable attention for supplementing the operation time of the devices' batteries.1-6 A typical piezoelectric energy harvester based on mechanical vibration can achieve maximum output power when its mass oscillates at its resonant frequency. However, the resonant frequency is commonly too high to be able to harvest energy from ambient vibration or human motion at low frequency.7 For low-frequency operation, several methods have been studied. Impact-type810and non-impact-type1113 frequency up-conversion techniques were proposed to convert a low-frequency input into a high-frequency input to a harvester with a high resonant frequency. In addition, a bistable for low-frequency operation. These harvesters effectively utilized low-frequency input, however, durability issues,810,15 structural complexity,1113 and limitation of input frequency or acceleration11-14 still limited their application to ambient vibration or human motion harvesting.

In this study, for extremely low frequency operation, we developed a flexible energy harvester that can accumulate potential energy through deformation of an elastic structure and convert it into kinetic energy in the form of resonant oscillation. The structural flexibility makes the harvester easy to deform by small forces such that it can be attached even to a curved surface.15181 It can harvest energy effectively from mechanical motion or deflection regardless of the frequency or velocity of the input motion, as long as the amount of motion or deformation is larger than the threshold value; furthermore, the harvester does not have any lower limit of the input motion frequency. The threshold deformation, which is related to the maximum output voltage, can be easily adjusted by adjusting the magnetic force.

Fig. 1(a) shows the schematic diagram of the fabricated energy harvester. It is composed of a piezoelectric cantilever, a flexible substrate, an anchor that fixes one end of the cantilever to the substrate, and parts for binding the free, opposite end of the cantilever to the substrate. The working principle of the harvester is shown in Figs. 1(b) and 1(c). When an external bending moment and/or force are applied to the substrate, the substrate and the cantilever deform together (Fig. 1(b)) until the bend radius of the harvester becomes identical to the threshold radius of curvature. This is because the cantilever is bound to the substrate by magnetic force and the elastic restoring force of the cantilever does not exceed the magnetic force. If the bend radius becomes smaller than the threshold radius of curvature, the elastic restoring force of the cantilever overcomes the magnetic attraction force. When this happens, the cantilever is released instantly from the substrate and oscillates at its resonant frequency (Fig. 1(c)).

FIG. 2. (a) Photographs of fabricated harvesters using magnet as binding mechanisms. The cantilever and substrate were bent together by means of the attraction force from two magnets. (b) Schematic diagram of experimental setup.

Fig. 2(a) shows photographs of the fabricated harvester. The flexible substrate and the lower layer of the cantilever of the prototype harvester were fabricated using a flexible polyvinyl chloride (PVC) film, and the upper layer of the cantilever was fabricated using piezoelectric polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) film; two neodymium magnets were to bind the substrate and the cantilever together. The cantilever measures $5 0 \mathrm { m m }$ in length, 10 mm in width, and $1 . 1 1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ in thickness (1 mm-thick PVC film plus $0 . 1 1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ -thick PVDF film). The fabricated cantilever was anchored onto a flexible PVC substrate by using another PVC film that was cut into a size of $1 0 \mathrm { m m } \times 1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ .

Fig. 2(b) shows the experimental setup for evaluating the performance of the fabricated energy harvester. A mechanical shaker was used to apply controllable bending to the harvester. The amplitude of the shaker displacement was magnified using a lever. In order to measure the input force, a load cell was placed on the lever. The harvester was mounted on a jig, and the substrate of the harvester was connected to the load cell through a wire. The motion frequency and amplitude of the shaker displacement were controlled by a function generator such that the bending of the flexible substrate exceeded the threshold radius of curvature of the piezoelectric cantilever. The open-circuit output voltage was monitored by an oscilloscope.

When the piezoelectric cantilever is mechanically deformed, the output voltage of the harvester is proportional to the strain rate of the piezoelectric material. When one of two parameters—the vibration amplitude and frequency—is given, the strain rate of the piezoelectric material is proportional to the other parameter. In our harvester, the vibration amplitude of the cantilever is determined by the radius of curvature at the moment of the release of the cantilever from the substrate, and the radius of curvature, in turn, depends on the magnetic force and the stiffness of the cantilever. In addition, the resonant frequency of the cantilever is not affected by input frequency or acceleration. Therefore, if the magnetic force is identical, the constant maximum output voltage appears regardless of the input frequency and there is no lower limit of applicable input frequency.

Fig. 3 shows the voltage outputs from the harvester for different frequency inputs when the strain rate of the piezoelectric cantilever is constant. During operation, the measured input force was $1 . 8 \mathrm { N }$ Fig. 3(a) shows a comparison of the output voltages for input frequencies of 2 and $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ The waveform of the output voltage oscillates at the resonant frequency of the cantilever. When the bent substrate of the harvester returned to the original flat shape, an additional peak was formed owing to the reattachment of the two magnets. As shown in the output voltage with input frequency of $2 \mathrm { H z }$ , however, when the substrate returned to the initial flat state before the cantilever vibration decayed completely, the cantilever reattached to the substrate because of the magnetic attraction force and it stopped vibration. Figs. 3(b) and 3(c) show the output voltages for four different input frequencies in the range of $2 \mathrm { H z }$ to $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . When the input frequency was reduced, the root mean square (RMS) voltage of the harvester decreased from $4 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ to $2 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ (Fig. 3(b)). However, the maximum peak of the output voltage remained almost constant regardless of the input frequency. For each input frequency tested, peak voltage was measured five times and the averages of the five obtained values were plotted together with error bars (Fig. 3(c)). The average of the total of 20 peak voltage values was $1 9 6 \mathrm { V }$ .

FIG. 3. (a) Output voltage response of fabricated harvester with input frequency of 2 and $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . The red dashed line in the graph is a waveform of the displacement from the mechanical shaker to deform the harvester's substrate. (b) The RMS voltage decreased as the input frequency decreased. ![](images/dfc8159c67b0448d956ecc2702d2f4a5aa541ffaa3c3188b4f9a5e8e3bb37ea9.jpg)  
FIG. 4. (a) Change in maximum peak voltage and threshold deformation with change in magnetic force induced by changing the number of magnets. When the magnetic force of the substrate was increased while keeping the resonant frequency of the cantilever, the radius of curvature at release decreased. (b) Output voltages for repeated bending motion. The moment of breakage was affected by the threshold radius of curvature. The fabricated harvester could be operated over 3900 cycles with a single magnet.

Fig. 4(a) shows the experimental results that verify the effect of increased magnetic force. When the magnetic force increases by magnets added on the substrate, the cantilever is released at a smaller radius of curvature, and the amplitude of the vibration of the cantilever increases. This in turn raises the strain rate of the piezoelectric material and thus the output voltage increases. When the number of magnets is tripled, the radius of curvature at release decreased from $3 9 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ to 20 mm and the peak voltage increased from $2 0 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ to $2 6 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ .

In order to verify the durability of the fabricated harvester, the output voltage was monitored for repeated cycles of bending motion. It was observed that a breakage occurred on the substrate that suffered from relatively larger deformation than the cantilever itself, and the lifetime of the harvester is reduced for a smaller threshold radius of curvature made by increased magnetic force. Fig. 4(b) shows the output voltages of three harvesters with different magnetic forces for repeated cycles of bending motion. With a single magnet on the substrate, the harvester could be operated over 3900 cycles. The result implies that by adjusting the magnetic force and reinforcing the substrate, it is possible to improve the durability of the proposed harvester. To determine the optimal load for achieving maximum power output, various resistive loads were tested, and the corresponding output voltage and power were plotted, as shown in Fig. 5. The maximum and average power at $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ of input frequency were $1 . 6 \mathrm { m W }$ and $3 4 . 0 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for a resistive load of $1 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ .

![](images/53cfb6317e8af4a40afc0030f4bf0e6020dc1431292fe6513b68c7bddee2a958.jpg)  
FIG. 5. Output voltage and power of fabricated harvester at various resistive loads. The maximum and average power at $0 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ of input frequency were $1 . 6 \mathrm { m W }$ and $3 4 . 0 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for a resistive load of $1 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ .

In conclusion, this paper proposed a frequency upconversion mechanism as a basis for a flexible energy harvester that converts deformation of the device itself into vibration of the device. Unlike previously developed vibration energy harvesters, the proposed harvester is not affected by the frequency or velocity of the input motion. Because the proposed harvester operates only via the accumulation of strain energy, it is possible to harvest energy from extremely low input frequencies without decreasing the output voltage. The accumulated strain energy is inversely proportional to the radius of curvature when the cantilever is released from the substrate of the harvester, and the threshold deformation can be adjusted by modifying the magnetic attraction force.
